title: Let `aggregate = TRUE` sort alphabetically
description:
Currently `aggregate = TRUE` aggregates stacks by names. I would personally expect it to also sort the stack by names, as per Brendan Gregg's description of a flame graph. This appears to not be the case:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3c69d1da-2c8b-41c3-bd76-209ad4a99554)

This can be confusing:

- Looking at a particular block, the empty area above it -- i.e. the area where it's not calling something else -- is positioned differently for every block, rather than always at the beginning or the end.
- Comparing different traces can be difficult, since the location of a particular call block, relative to others with the same caller, can change between runs.

Compare to the below, created from the same profiling data, but with the stacks sorted by names:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/800af1c8-3bab-4400-90b9-6bfb2427024a)

Produced with the hacked-together code below, which splits `profvis` in two, to work on the profile data before widget creation:

```r
# profvis, but returning data instead of widget
profdat <- function(
  expr,
  interval = 0.01,
  prof_output = NULL,
  prof_input = NULL,
  timing = NULL,
  split = c("h", "v"),
  torture = 0,
  simplify = TRUE,
  rerun = FALSE
) {
  rlang::check_exclusive(expr, prof_input)
  split <- match.arg(split)
  # profvis::profvis code...
  message <- profvis:::parse_rprof_lines(lines, expr_source)
  message$prof_output <- prof_output
  message$highlight <- profvis:::highlightPatterns()
  message$split <- split
  message
}

# remaining part of profvis
profshow <- function(message, width = NULL, height = NULL) {
  htmlwidgets::createWidget(
    name = "profvis",
    list(message = message),
    width = width,
    height = height,
    package = "profvis",
    sizingPolicy = htmlwidgets::sizingPolicy(
      padding = 0,
      browser.fill = TRUE,
      viewer.suppress = TRUE,
      knitr.defaultWidth = "100%",
      knitr.defaultHeight = "600px",
      knitr.figure = FALSE
    )
  )
}

# icycle = TRUE inverts the depths, to make something like an "icycle graph"
# location = TRUE doesn't aggregate calls to the same function with different file/line information
block <- function(message, icycle = FALSE, location = TRUE) {
  x <- message$prof # stack table
  if ((rx <- nrow(x)) == 0)
    return(x)
  if (!location) {
    x$filenum[] <- NA
    x$linenum[] <- NA
    x$filename[] <- NA
  }
  x <- sort_by(x, ~ time + depth)
  nt <- max(x$time)

  # rearrange traces
  if (icycle) {
    ds <- x$depth
    inds <- unlist(tapply(seq_len(nrow(x)), x$time, rev))
    x <- x[inds, , drop = FALSE]
    x$depth <- ds
  }
  md <- max(x$depth)
  depths <- seq_len(md)
  depths <- rev(depths)
  mtds <- unlist(tapply(x$depth, x$time, max))

  for (d in depths) {
    empty <- mtds < d
    relevant <- subset(x, depth == d)
    sortable <- relevant[c("label", "filenum", "linenum", "filename")]
    nonempty_ord <- do.call(
      order,
      c(
        unname(sortable),
        list(na.last = FALSE)
      )
    )
    ord <- c(which(empty), which(!empty)[nonempty_ord])
    x$time <- match(x$time, ord)
    x <- sort_by(x, ~ time)
    mtds <- mtds[ord]
  }

  x <- x[order(x$time), , drop = FALSE]
  row.names(x) <- NULL
  message$prof <- x
  message
}

# pd <- profdat(expr, ...)
# profshow(pd, ...) # same as profvis(expr, ...)
# profshow(block(pd), ...) # aggregates and sorts by name
```

title: digest() times are attributed to other functions
description:
When calling `digest::digest()`, sometimes the times can be attributed to other functions. This is likely due to something funny in the R profiler itself, but I'm filing it here to track it.

To start, this example correctly attributes the time spent in `digest()`, about 700ms on my machine:

```R
profvis::profvis({
  x <- list(1,2,3)
  for (i in 1:5000) {
    digest::digest(x)
  }
})
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/86978/40140702-8ccc7aa4-5921-11e8-9dfb-ccafb9c52579.png)

If you profile `file.exists()`, it's much faster -- this takes about 10ms on my machine:

```R
profvis::profvis({
  for (i in 1:5000) {
    file.exists("abcd")
  }
})
```


However, if the `digest()` is followed by `file.exists()`, profvis says that most of the time is spent in `file.exists()`:

```R
profvis::profvis({
  x <- list(1,2,3)
  for (i in 1:5000) {
    digest::digest(x)
    file.exists("abcd")
  }
})
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/86978/40140596-5aac030a-5921-11e8-9324-68a44b93a5ce.png)


If the Rprof output is saved with the `prof_output` arg, most of the lines do indeed say that they're in `file.exists()`.

title: Profile non-cpu time?
description: **Feature Request**: It would be really helpful to support a mode where CPU and non-CPU time is measured. **Details**: From `Rprof`: "How time is measured varies by platform: on a Unix-alike it is the CPU time of the R process, so for example excludes time when R is waiting for input or for processes run by system to return." Therefore, consider: ```{r} system.time(download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/sparklyr/master/inst/extdata/install_spark.csv", destfile = tempfile())) ``` with output: ``` trying URL 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/sparklyr/master/inst/extdata/install_spark.csv' Content type 'text/plain; charset=utf-8' length 2534 bytes ================================================== downloaded 2534 bytes user system elapsed 0.017 0.004 0.423 ``` However, profiling: ```{r} profvis::profvis(download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstudio/sparklyr/master/inst/extdata/install_spark.csv", destfile = tempfile())) ``` yields, `20ms`: while this is correct from `profvis` use of `Rprof`, R is often used to proxy to other processes that users would want to be able to profile as well. Including an option to include the whole execution time without excluding IO calls, would be really helpful. That said, this probably requires a change in `Rprof` and `R` itself. Never the less, opening this feature request to discuss this further.

title: Partially aggregated samples of repeated function calls
description:
In my use cases, I call a lot of fast functions repeatedly, and flame graphs help me understand how the computation times adds up. I like `pprof` because the flame graphs fully aggregate the samples of each function. Below, it is easy to see that `h()` is more of a bottleneck than `g()`.

```r
f <- function(...) {
  file <- tempfile()
  g(file)
  h(file)
  unlink(file)
  invisible()
}

g <- function(file) {
  writeLines("lorem ipsum", file)
}

h <- function(file) {
  digest::digest(file)
}

rprof <- tempfile()
pprof <- tempfile()
Rprof(filename = rprof)
replicate(1e3, f())
Rprof(NULL)
samples <- profile::read_rprof(rprof)
profile::write_pprof(samples, pprof)
system2(
  "/home/landau/go/bin/pprof",
  c("-http", "0.0.0.0:8080", pprof)
```

title: Performance: profvis(prof_input = large_file)
description:
I am profiling [`drake`](https://github.com/ropensci/drake) on a large test case. `profvis(prof_output = "make_rprof_4096_64.Rprof")` generates raw output just fine, but when I try `profvis(prof_input = "make_rprof_4096_64.Rprof")` in the RStudio IDE, the point-and-click responsiveness is prohibitively slow (on a mid-range Linux desktop computer).

Are there plans to enhance the scalability of `profvis`? When I convert the files to `proto` format for `pprof` and then run `pprof -http=:8080 make_rprof_4096_64.proto`, the interactive flame graph is super responsive.

```r
# Profile the overhead incurred by drake on a large example.

n <- 4096
max_deps <- floor(sqrt(n))

# remotes::install_github("ropensci/drake")
library(drake)
library(fs)
library(profile)

# Let n be the number of targets.
# If max_deps is Inf, there are n * (n - 1) / 2 dependency connections
# among all the targets (maximum possible edges)
# For i = 2, ..., n, target i depends on targets 1 through i - 1.
create_plan <- function(n, max_deps = sqrt(n)) {
  plan <- drake_plan(target_1 = 1)
  for (i in seq_len(n - 1) + 1){
    target <- paste0("target_", i)
    dependencies <- paste0("target_", tail(seq_len(i - 1), max_deps))
    command <- paste0("max(", paste0(dependencies, collapse = ", "), ")")
    plan <- rbind(plan, data.frame(target = target, command = command))
  }
  plan
}

config_rprof <- function(n, max_deps = sqrt(n)) {
  paste0("config_rprof_", n, "_", max_deps, ".Rprof")
}

make_rprof <- function(n, max_deps = sqrt(n)) {
  paste0("make_rprof_", n, "_", max_deps, ".Rprof")
}

overhead <- function(n, max_deps = sqrt(n)) {
  plan <- create_plan(n = n, max_deps = max_deps)
  cache <- new_cache(tempfile())
  profvis::profvis(
    config <- drake_config(plan = plan, cache = cache, verbose = 0L),
    prof_output = config_rprof(n, max_deps)
  )
  profvis::profvis(
    make(config = config),
    prof_output = make_rprof(n, max_deps)
  )
}

overhead(n, max_deps) # Could take a long time

# Convert profiling results to pprof-friendly format.
for(path in c(config_rprof(n, max_deps), make_rprof(n, max_deps))) {
  proto <- path_ext_set(path, "proto")
  data <- read_rprof(path)
  write_pprof(data, proto)
}
```

title: Cells with `[<-` are not properly highlighted and linked
Filtering references to console outside of profvis call()
description:
## The problem

If any functions are defined at the console (as opposed to in a file) but outside of the `profvis({ })` block, the profiler output does not include information to tell which expression the call came from. For example, if you run this code:

``` r eval=FALSE
f <- function() { pause(0.1) }
g <- function() {
  f()
}
profvis({

  g()
}, prof_output = "temp.prof")
```

The profiler output in temp.prof might look like this (irrelevant stuff has been trimmed):

```
#File 1: 
"pause" 1#1 "f" 1#2 "g" 1#3
```

So even though `f()` and `pause()` were called from code that was outside of `profvis({ })`, all of the lines of code are reported to be from a file with no name. When calculating the time taken for each line of code in `<expr>`, for this line of code profvis will report that there was one sample on line 1, one sample on line 2, and one sample on line 3, even though the time spent on lines 1 and 2 were in expressions that were completely outside the `profvis({ })` call.

Additionally, if one of the external functions was long, it might result in, say a `1#10` in the profiler output. But there's no line 10 in the `<expr>` that profvis has, so this would result in an error when it's displayed.
## The current workaround

The current workaround is to use the following heuristic to filter out line number references to `<expr>`:
- Search for the label (like "pause" or "f") in the `<expr>` code at that line. If the label is found, then count that sample toward that line's total time. If not found, don't count the time.
- Do the same if the label is "<Anonymous>", because anonymous functions by definition won't have their text in that line of code.

This strategy is prone to false positives. Even if the code is defined outside of `<expr>`, the text of the label might happen to be in that line of code. Similarly, an anonymous function might be called outside of `<expr>`.

It's also prone to false negatives. Sometimes a function label is not the same as the text in that line of code, as is the case for functions like `[<-`. Sometimes an expression spans lines of code, but only the first line is reported in the profiler. In the code below, line #2 of the `<expr>`, the line with `identity(`, will be reported to take the time, but the time is really spent in line #3, with `g()`.

``` r eval=FALSE
f <- function() { pause(0.1) }
g <- function() {
  f()
}
profvis({
  identity(
    g()
  )
}, prof_output = "temp.prof")
```

The output:

```
#File 1: 
"pause" 1#1 "f" 1#2 "g" "identity" 1#2
```
## Solution

The solution is to change the `srcfile` attribute in the expression passed to `profvis()` from `""` to `"<expr>". That way, the profiler will output something like this:

```
#File 1: 
#File 2: <expr>
"pause" 1#1 "f" 1#2 "g" 2#3
```

title: In Data pane, "Calls" column title is misleading
description:
Consider this example:

``` R
profvis({
  pause2 <- pause
  pause3 <- pause

  for (i in 1:50) {
    pause(0.005)
    pause2(0.001)
    pause3(0.001)
  }
})
```

The code / flame graph pane:
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/86978/14994973/1f9588d2-1138-11e6-939b-4869ea0fffaa.png)

And the Data pane:
![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/86978/14994981/2bcec370-1138-11e6-9085-1fb81696cd99.png)

In the Data pane, it says there are 9, 2, and 6, calls to `pause`, `pause2`, and `pause3`, respectively, but in reality there are the same number of calls to each of the functions. The value in the Calls column is the number of cells in the flame graph for each function, where each cell is a set of consecutive samples that happen to be in the same function. However, the number of cells doesn't necessarily correspond to the number of times a function is called.

I tried thinking of another name for the Calls column that's more descriptive, but I couldn't come up with one. It may be better to not have that column at all.

title: Correctly filter out `profvis::prof` calls.
description:
Normally, when `prof()` is called, the label resolves to `"prof"`. When `profvis::prof()` is called, the label of the function resolves to `"<Anonymous>"`. This makes it fail to filter out the `prof`-related items on the call stack, because it looks for everything from the lowest `"force"` down to `"prof"`.

As a related problem, if `prof()` is called from any other function, the `prof`-related items on the stack also won't get filtered out. So it might be necessary to put a specially-named function on the stack and look for that.

title: Figure out what it means when a srcref is the first item in profiling output
description:
Suppose the file `test.R` contains this code:

```
f <- function(x) {
  x
}

for (i in 1:5e6) {
  i2 <- i * 2
  f(i2)
}
```

And it's profiled with:

``` R
Rprof("test.prof", line.profiling=TRUE)
source("test.R", keep.source = TRUE)
Rprof(NULL)

# Optional: visualize with:
profvis(profvis:::parse_rprof('test.prof'))
```

The output looks something like this:

```
line profiling: sample.interval=20000
#File 1: test.R
1#5 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#2 "f" 1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#7 "f" 1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
"*" 1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#7 "f" 1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
"*" 1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#2 "f" 1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#7 "f" 1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
"*" 1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
"*" 1#6 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
```

When a label (like `"f"`) is followed by a reference (like `1#7`), the reference indicates where the labeled function is called from.

But in the case where the very first item on a line is a reference, it seems to indicate something else, like what code is currently being eval'ed. This leads to some confusing output, like this line:

```
1#7 "f" 1#7 "eval" "eval" "withVisible" "source" 
```

It looks like when the first item is a reference, it simply prints out `R_Srcref` (line 229 below), whereas the other (later) references are all associated with a `cptr`, as in `cptr->srcref` (line 241):
https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/be7197f/src/main/eval.c#L228-L244

It may also be relevant that some built-in R functions don't put a frame on the call stack:
  https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help//2013-April/350964.html
